newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African markets shaky after bad money figures.
newsitem.headline: S.African markets shaky after bad money figures.

text.p: South African markets were looking shaky on Friday after worse-than-expected October money supply and private credit extension figures, analysts said.
The rand and long bonds both weakened further in after hours dealings, taking losses on the rand to more than three cents against the U.S. dollar since Thursday's close.
"Investors from overseas realise that high money supply and credit growth are not good for the currency," said Nick Barnardt, economist at BOE NatWest.
The Reserve Bank said year-on-year M3 money supply grew 15.96 percent in October while annual private sector credit growth was 18.86 percent, the highest level since July.
Both figures were worse than expected. A Reuters consensus poll of economists forecast M3 growth of 15.1 percent and private sector credit extension at 18.1.
Economists said it appeared Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals had good reason to expect the bad figures when he hiked the Bank rate last week to 17 from 16 percent.
Stals gave excess credit growth as a key reason for the increase, effective on November 21, which caught South African markets off guard.

High credit growth in October dovetails with other signals from the economy last month, notably a surge in new car sales to a 14-year high, prompted by pre-emptive buying ahead of anticipated price increases due to the rand's fall.
That had led economists to expect bad numbers, but the actual figures remained a nasty shock.
Most analysts expect credit growth to plateau now and slow sharply in the new year, but Barnardt said the market would now be edgy ahead of fresh data next week.
The week starts with October trade figures on Monday.
"If the trade figure is bad we could see bond yields above 16 percent," he said.

Other data next week includes October producer price inflation on Thursday, expected to rise to 7.9 percent year-on-year from 7.6 in September, and November reserves next Friday, expected to reach 10.38 billion rand from 10.28 billion.
